scope.start: 17b: Ravina's question to Rava about a *get* written and kept in the husband's pocket (18a opens mid-exchange)
scope.end: 18b: the man who told ten men to write a *get*, two signing that day and the rest ten days later, brought before R. Yehoshua ben Levi (answer on 19a)

sections.title: Does the Dating Ordinance Still Accomplish Anything?
sections.gist: Two final challenges to the requirement of a *zman* in a *get*: the husband who writes one and holds it, and *gittin* sent from overseas.

bullets.text: Behind the requirement of a *zman* stand two concerns: fixing when the divorce took effect so a wife cannot escape punishment for adultery, and protecting a buyer of the *peirot* of her *nichsei melog*.
Both challenges press the same point: when the date in the *get* does not match the moment the *get* actually took effect, what has the *takanah* achieved?

children.title: The Get Written and Left in His Pocket
children.gist: Ravina asks Rava about a husband who writes a *get* but holds onto it hoping for reconciliation; Rava answers that a person does not hasten his own calamity.

bullets.text: Ravina to Rava: the husband writes a *get* and puts it in his pocket without giving it, thinking that if she appeases him he will be appeased. When he finally gives it, the date is stale — did the Sages rule such a *get* may not be used?

Rava: a person does not hasten a calamity upon himself and will not ordinarily prepare a *get* in advance; he waits until he is ready to divorce. The scenario is unlikely, so the Sages saw no need to legislate for it.
The very act of writing signals resolve — one does not draft a *get* on the way to marriage counseling.

children.title: Gittin Arriving from Overseas
children.gist: A *get* written overseas in Nisan may reach the wife only in Tishrei; Rav Ashi answers that such documents are publicly known not to take effect from their date.

bullets.text: Ravina to Rav Ashi: *gittin* that come from a country overseas are written, say, in Nisan and do not reach the woman until Tishrei. What did the Sages accomplish with their ordinance to date the *get*?

Rav Ashi: concerning these, it is public knowledge (*kala it lehu*) that they do not take effect from the date on which they were written; so in a conflict over produce the husband sold, the woman must bring witnesses to testify when she received her *get*.
Rashi: the gap raises concerns of both *zenut* and *peirot*, and in both the burden falls on her to establish affirmatively when the *get* reached her hand.

sections.title: When Do the Three Months Begin: Writing or Giving?
sections.gist: Rav and Shmuel dispute from which moment a divorced woman counts the three months before remarrying; an objection, two supporting baraitot, and the final ruling.

chart.caption: Rav and Shmuel on the start of the three-month wait
rows: An agent tarries three months on the road
She must still wait three months from delivery
Rav Pappa; Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
A *get* deposited with a trustee, to be given only after three months
She may marry immediately when it is given
Rav Kahana; Rav Pappi; Rav Ashi — and the *halakha*

children.title: Rav vs. Shmuel and the Two Women in One Courtyard
children.gist: Rav counts from the giving and Shmuel from the writing; Rav Natan bar Hoshaya objects that Shmuel splits two women divorced at the same moment, and Abaye answers that each document's date speaks for itself.

bullets.text: The Sages prohibited a woman from remarrying within three months of divorce or widowhood, to prevent doubt over a child's paternity.
Rav: count from the time of the giving of the *get*. Shmuel: count from the time of its writing.

Rav Natan bar Hoshaya objects to Shmuel: two women in one courtyard receive their *gittin* at the same moment, but one document was written earlier — on Shmuel's view one is still forbidden to remarry and the other is already permitted.
Abaye: this is no difficulty — the date on each document proves its own case, so for each woman it is clear whether she may remarry yet.

children.title: The Baraita Taught in Accordance with Rav
children.gist: An agent delayed three months on the road: she must still wait three months from when the *get* reaches her hand.

bullets.text: Baraita: one who sends a *get* to his wife and the agent tarries three months on the way — once it reaches her hand she must wait three months before remarrying.
No concern here of a *get yashan*, since the husband was not secluded with her while the *get* was being delivered.
*Get yashan* is not a matter of calendar age but of seclusion: if he was with her after the writing, we infer he may have reconsidered the divorce.

children.title: The Baraita Taught in Accordance with Shmuel
children.gist: A *get* deposited with a trustee to be given only after three months: when it is given she may marry at once.

bullets.text: Baraita: one about to travel deposits a *get* with a trustee and says, give it to her only after three months — once he gives it to her she may marry immediately, with no further waiting.
Here too there is no concern of a *get yashan*, as he was not secluded with her in the interim.

children.title: Practice of the Later Amoraim and the Halachah
children.gist: Amoraim split in practice, and the *halakha* is fixed from the time of writing.

bullets.text: Rav Kahana, Rav Pappi and Rav Ashi would in practice count the three months from the writing; Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua counted from the giving.
*Vehilkhata* — the counting begins from the time of writing.

sections.title: When Does Shemittah Cancel a Ketubah?
sections.gist: A *ketubah* is not an ordinary loan, so the question is at what point it turns into a plain debt that the Sabbatical Year cancels — Rav requiring two acts, Shmuel either one.

bullets.text: A *ketubah* is a *tenai beit din*, imposed by the Sages as a condition of marriage rather than contracted privately, and as such is not treated as an ordinary cancellable debt.
The live question is the case where the marriage has ended and the *ketubah* is collectible but unpaid: has it migrated into the domain of ordinary private debt?

chart.caption: Rav and Shmuel: which acts turn a *ketubah* into a debt that *shemittah* cancels
columns: *Zekifah* alone (established as a debt in court)

children.title: Rav: Both Pegimah and Zekifah; Shmuel: Either One
children.gist: Rav requires that she both collect partial payment and establish the rest as a debt in court; Shmuel holds either act alone suffices.

bullets.text: The Gemara's question: from when is the debt established by a marriage contract cancelled in the Sabbatical Year?
Rav: it becomes like a debt, and is cancelled, only from when the woman collects partial payment and establishes the rest as a debt in court.
Shmuel: it occurs either when she collects partial payment though she did not establish it as a debt, or when she establishes the whole value as a debt in court though she collected nothing.
Concretely: on a 200-*zuz* *ketubah*, taking 50 as partial collection of the *ketubah* is *pegimah*; telling him to hold the remaining 150 as a loan he owes her is *zekifah*.
Rav's position is the more demanding one: only when both steps have been taken has the obligation left the domain of *tenai beit din* for that of ordinary debt.

children.title: The Baraita Taught in Accordance with Rav
children.gist: A baraita states outright that neither *pegimah* nor *zekifah* alone cancels the *ketubah*.

bullets.text: Baraita: from when is the debt of a *ketubah* cancelled? From when she accepts partial payment and establishes the rest as a debt in court.
It continues: if she accepted partial payment but did not establish the debt, or established the debt but accepted no partial payment, it is not cancelled until she does both.

children.title: The Baraita Taught in Accordance with Shmuel
children.gist: A baraita lists women's claims cancelled by *shemittah* once established as a loan, and defines that moment as standing trial.

bullets.text: Baraita: the fine and damages of a rapist, the fine of one who falsely claims his wife was not a virgin, the fine for seduction, and the debt of a woman's *ketubah* — if established as a loan, the Sabbatical Year cancels them; if not, it does not.
From when are they considered established as a loan? From the time of standing trial, since the abstract obligation becomes a debt once the court has ruled that one must pay.
This baraita mentions only *zekifah* and is silent about *pegimah*, so it supports only one leg of Shmuel's position and does not show that *pegimah* alone suffices.
Unlike the other disputes on the daf, the Gemara issues no ruling here between Rav and Shmuel.

sections.title: A Ketubah Written by Day and Signed at Night
sections.gist: Shmuel likens a *ketubah* to a court enactment; R. Chiya bar Rav's *ketubah* seems to show Rav agrees, but the Gemara traces the leniency to the scribe and witnesses remaining engaged in the matter.

bullets.text: Shmuel: a *ketubah* is considered like a court enactment — just as court enactments may be written by day and signed at night without the gap invalidating them, so may a *ketubah*.
R. Chiya bar Rav's *ketubah* was written by day and signed at night, and Rav was there and said nothing, which suggests he agrees with Shmuel.
The Gemara rejects the proof: there the scribe and witnesses were continuously engaged in that same matter, from the daytime writing until the signing at night.

Baraita of R. Elazar bar R. Tzadok: a document written by day and signed at night is invalid only when they were not continuously engaged in the matter; if they were engaged in it until nightfall, it is valid.
This leniency does not stretch indefinitely — once the gap widens or the parties are no longer occupied with the same proceeding, the concern returns.

sections.title: Rabbi Shimon's Validation of a Get Signed at Night
sections.gist: Rava explains R. Shimon's reason, and Reish Lakish and R. Yochanan dispute how long a delay between writing and signing his leniency covers.

children.title: Rava: Once He Decided to Divorce, the Produce Is No Longer His
children.gist: R. Shimon validates a *get* written by day and signed at night because the husband's rights to the produce end at the writing.

bullets.text: The mishnah taught that R. Shimon deems valid a *get* written during the day and signed at night.

Rava: R. Shimon holds that once the husband has decided to divorce her he no longer has rights to the produce of her property, and writing the *get* shows that he has decided; the woman therefore acquires the produce from the moment of writing, whenever the signing took place.
*Keivan shenatan einav legarshah shuv ein lo piyus* — from the writing his resolve is treated as irreversible, so an earlier date in the document does no practical harm.

children.title: How Long a Gap? Reish Lakish vs. Rabbi Yochanan
children.gist: Reish Lakish limits R. Shimon's leniency to signing that same night, fearing reconciliation; R. Yochanan extends it to ten days, since reconciliation would be public knowledge.

bullets.text: Reish Lakish: R. Shimon deems such a *get* valid only when it is signed immediately, that night after the writing; but not when the signing is delayed up to ten days later.
The reason: we are concerned that perhaps he appeased his wife and lived with her in the interim, which would invalidate the *get*.
R. Yochanan: even a delay of up to ten days is valid for R. Shimon, because if he had appeased her the matter would become public knowledge and everyone would hear of it.

illustration.caption: The window R. Shimon's leniency covers: signing the same night, or up to ten days later. Reish Lakish fears *shema piyes*; R. Yochanan answers that reconciliation would be public knowledge.

sections.title: "Write a Get for My Wife": Said to Ten Men
sections.gist: R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute whether the extra signers of a *get* are witnesses or merely fulfilling the husband's stipulation, and the Gemara spells out what turns on it.

chart.caption: What turns on whether the extra signers are witnesses or fulfill a stipulation
columns: Two sign that day, the rest ten days later
One of the ten is a relative or disqualified
rows: Two function as witnesses; the rest sign only due to the husband's stipulation
Valid — two witnesses signed the day of writing and the stipulation was fulfilled
Valid — he was not serving as a witness, and two qualified witnesses signed
Invalid — not all the witnesses signed on the day of writing
Invalid — as whenever one of a group of witnesses is disqualified

children.title: The Dispute and Its Case: When He Said *Kulchem*
children.gist: The dispute is set in the case where the husband said "all of you," since otherwise a mishnah already rules that one writes and two sign.

bullets.text: R. Yochanan: he means that all of them should sign — two function as witnesses and all the rest sign only due to his stipulation, since he made the *get* dependent on all of them signing, not on ten serving as witnesses.
Reish Lakish: all of them function as witnesses.

The Gemara clarifies the case: if he did not say "all of you," a mishnah (66b) already teaches that one writes and two sign. The dispute is where he said *kulchem* — one writes and everyone else must sign.
Rashi: where he gathers ten without saying *kulchem*, his purpose is to publicize the divorce; the document itself still bears only the two standard witnesses.
On R. Yochanan's view the document shows two signing as *ed* with the other eight signatures beneath; on Reish Lakish's, every one of the ten signs as *ed*.

children.title: First Difference: Two Sign Today, the Rest Ten Days Later
children.gist: Staggered signing is fine if the extra signatures only fulfill a stipulation, but fatal if all ten are witnesses.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks what difference it makes whether the rest function as witnesses or only fulfill the husband's stipulation.

One difference: two signed on the day the *get* was written and the rest only up to ten days later. For the stipulation view it is valid — two witnesses signed the day of writing and the stipulation was also fulfilled.
For the view that all sign as witnesses it is invalid, since not all the witnesses signed on the day the *get* was written.
A *tenai* carries no fixed time; a condition may be fulfilled whenever the parties get to it, whereas witnesses to a *get* must sign together.

returns_to.note: The same ten-day window debated for R. Shimon's leniency

children.title: Second Difference: One of the Ten Is Disqualified
children.gist: A relative or otherwise disqualified signer ruins the *get* only if all ten are witnesses; within R. Yochanan's view there is a further split about a disqualified man who signed first.

bullets.text: Another difference: one of the ten turns out to be a relative of the husband or wife, or otherwise disqualified. For the stipulation view the *get* is valid — he did not serve as a witness, and the document bears the signatures of two qualified witnesses.
For the view that all sign as witnesses it is invalid, as whenever one member of a group of witnesses is disqualified.

Within R. Yochanan's view, if the disqualified man signed at the beginning, before two valid witnesses: some say valid, since the ten are only fulfilling a stipulation and it makes no difference whether he signed first or last.
Some say invalid, out of concern that courts will confuse it with ordinary documents and come to rely on disqualified witnesses there.

sections.title: The Case Before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sections.gist: A real case of ten men told to write a *get*, two signing that day and the rest up to ten days later, comes before R. Yehoshua ben Levi.

bullets.text: A certain man said to ten men: write a *get* for my wife. Two of them signed that day and the others signed after a delay of up to ten days.
He came before R. Yehoshua ben Levi to ask what the *halakha* is with regard to such a *get*, and R. Yehoshua ben Levi began his answer.
The case joins the two threads of the daf: R. Shimon's tolerance of a gap between writing and signing, and the dispute over the role of the extra signers.
*Mishum iguna akilu bah rabbanan* — where a woman would otherwise be left an *agunah*, authorities may lean on lenient opinions they would not adopt *lechatchilah*.

returns_to.note: Relies on the ten-day window disputed by Reish Lakish and R. Yochanan
The case of ten men told to write a get

sections.continues: Continues on 19a: R. Yehoshua ben Levi answers that R. Shimon is worthy of being relied upon in exigent circumstances, and the Gemara shows that he follows R. Yochanan on the delayed signing but Reish Lakish on all ten functioning as witnesses.

judgment_calls: Grouped the pocketed *get* and the overseas *get* under one parent section, since both are challenges to what the dating ordinance accomplishes; each could have stood as its own top-level unit.

Kept the *ketubah*–*ma'aseh beit din* discussion (written by day, signed at night) as a top-level section rather than nesting it under the *shemittah* discussion; both concern the *ketubah*, but this one belongs to the daf's writing-and-signing thread, which it leads into.

Made R. Shimon's leniency (Rava; Reish Lakish vs. R. Yochanan) and the ten-men dispute separate top-level sections, with the closing story linked back to both by *returns_to*; an alternative was to nest the ten-men dispute under R. Shimon's leniency, since the ten-day window recurs there.
Split the two baraitot on the three-month count into separate children rather than one 'two baraitot' child, so each supporting case reads on its own; the chart ties them back together.
coverage_notes: The shiur opens with a review of 17b material (R. Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on the purpose of the *zman*, R. Shimon and the *get mukdam*, the three invalid *gittin*, writing without a date, cutting out the date, and vague dating). That precedes the scope of this daf (which begins with Ravina's question to Rava at 17b.13); only brief framing from it is retained.

The essay says the later amoraim who counted from the writing were 'Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi'; the text has Rav Kahana, Rav Pappi and Rav Ashi (from writing) against Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua (from giving). Followed the text.
The essay attributes the 'continuously engaged in the same matter' baraita to a tanna of the school of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi; the text has Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok. Followed the text.
The essay repeatedly calls the sage who heard the ten-signers case 'Rabbi Shimon ben Levi'; the text has Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Followed the text.

The essay lists the categories in the Shmuel-baraita as *ones*, *knas*, *pitui* and *ketuvat isha*; the text lists the rapist's fine and damages, the fine of one who falsely claims his wife was not a virgin, the fine for seduction, and the *ketubah*. Followed the text.
The shiur's discussion of R. Yehoshua ben Levi's actual ruling, *sha'at hadechak* and Rashi's examples of hardship belongs to 19a and is noted in the `continues` field rather than outlined here.
